fact: **Bending moment is maximum where the shear force is zero (or changes sign).**
detail: Because dM/dx = V. Equally: **dV/dx = −w**. So the SF diagram is one degree higher than the load diagram, and the BM diagram one degree higher than the SF diagram.

fact: A **point of contraflexure** is where the **bending moment changes sign** (passes through zero).
detail: Not where shear is zero — that is where BM is *maximum*. A simply supported beam with no overhang has **no** point of contraflexure; an overhanging or continuous beam does.

fact: Simply supported beam: **central point load W → M = WL/4**; **UDL w → M = wL²/8**.
detail: Cantilever: **point load at free end → M = WL**; **UDL → M = wL²/2**. Fixed beam with UDL: **wL²/12 at supports, wL²/24 at mid-span**.

fact: Under a **UDL** the SF diagram is a **straight sloping line** and the BM diagram a **parabola**.
detail: Under a **point load** the SF is constant (steps at the load) and the BM linear. Under a **triangular** load the SF is parabolic and the BM cubic.

fact: **Poisson's ratio μ = lateral strain / longitudinal strain**; for steel **≈ 0.3**, concrete 0.15–0.20, cork ≈ 0.
detail: Thermodynamic limits are **0 to 0.5**; at exactly 0.5 the material is **incompressible** (rubber ≈ 0.5). It has **no units**.
For steel with μ = 0.3: **G = E/2.6 ≈ 0.385E** and **K = E/1.2 ≈ 0.833E**. So **E > K > G** for ordinary metals — a quick sanity check on any computed value.

fact: **Principal stresses σ₁,₂ = (σx+σy)/2 ± √[((σx−σy)/2)² + τ²]**; **τ_max = √[((σx−σy)/2)² + τ²]**.
detail: Shear stress is **zero on a principal plane**, and the two principal planes are **90° apart**. The planes of **maximum shear** lie at **45° to the principal planes**.

fact: On **Mohr's circle**, an angle **2θ** on the circle corresponds to **θ** on the element.
detail: The circle's **centre is at (σx+σy)/2** and its **radius equals τ_max**. For **pure shear**, σ₁ = +τ and σ₂ = −τ — which is why a brittle shaft in torsion fails on a **45° helix**.

fact: **Strain energy: U = σ²V/2E** (gradual load); **impact/sudden load gives twice the stress** of a gradual one.
detail: **Resilience** is the energy absorbed up to the elastic limit; **proof resilience** is that at the elastic limit; **modulus of resilience** is proof resilience per unit volume. **Toughness** is the total area under the stress-strain curve.

fact: **Thermal stress σ = αEΔT** — and it arises **only if the member is restrained**.
detail: A **free** member expands with **no stress at all**. For a **composite** bar, each material carries a different stress and equilibrium requires the forces to be equal and opposite. Steel α ≈ 12 × 10⁻⁶/°C.

fact: **Flexure formula: M/I = σ/y = E/R.**
detail: Assumes the material is **homogeneous, isotropic, obeys Hooke's law**, the beam is **initially straight** with a **constant cross-section**, plane sections **remain plane**, and the load acts in a **plane of symmetry**.

fact: **Shear stress distribution: τ = VAȳ/(Ib)** — parabolic in a rectangle, **maximum at the neutral axis**.
detail: For a **rectangle τ_max = 1.5 × τ_avg**; for a **circle 1.33 × τ_avg**. Bending stress is maximum at the **extreme fibre** and zero at the NA — exactly the opposite distribution.

fact: **Euler: P_cr = π²EI/L_e²** — valid only for **long** columns.
detail: Effective length: **both ends hinged L**, **both fixed L/2**, **one fixed one free 2L**, **one fixed one hinged L/√2**. So a fixed-fixed column carries **four times** the load of a pinned-pinned one of the same length.

fact: **Rankine: 1/P = 1/P_c + 1/P_e** — valid for **both short and long** columns.
detail: That universality is Rankine's advantage over Euler, which is unsafe for short columns (it predicts an absurdly high load as L → 0). A column buckles about its axis of **minimum** radius of gyration.

fact: **Torsion: T/J = τ/r = Gθ/L.** Polar modulus for a solid circle **Z_p = πd³/16**.
detail: Shear stress in torsion is **zero at the centre and maximum at the surface** — which is why a **hollow** shaft is so efficient. **GJ** is the torsional rigidity, the analogue of **EI**.

fact: Static determinacy of a truss: **m = 2j − 3** (plane truss).
detail: **m < 2j−3** unstable (deficient); **m = 2j−3** determinate and stable; **m > 2j−3** indeterminate (redundant). For a **space** truss the relation is m = 3j − 6.

fact: Truss analysis: **method of joints** for all members, **method of sections** for a few specific ones.
detail: Method of joints needs a joint with **not more than two unknowns**. Method of sections cuts through **not more than three** unknown members. **Zero-force members** occur at unloaded two-member joints and at unloaded three-member joints where two are collinear.

fact: A **three-hinged arch is determinate**; a two-hinged arch is indeterminate to the first degree.
detail: For a three-hinged parabolic arch, the **horizontal thrust H = wL²/(8h)** under a UDL — it varies **inversely with the rise**. A flatter arch thrusts harder.

fact: **Macaulay's method** integrates the BM equation using terms that vanish when negative.
detail: Standard deflections: **central point load δ = WL³/48EI**; **UDL δ = 5wL⁴/384EI**; **cantilever point load WL³/3EI**; **cantilever UDL wL⁴/8EI**. Note the deflection varies as **L³ or L⁴** — doubling the span multiplies deflection 8- or 16-fold.

fact: **Mohr's theorems (moment-area)**: θ = area of M/EI diagram; δ = moment of that area about the point.
detail: Most efficient for **cantilevers** and for beams with a **simple M/EI diagram**. The **conjugate beam** method restates the same idea: load a fictitious beam with M/EI and read off shear as slope and moment as deflection.

fact: **Castigliano's theorem: δ = ∂U/∂P** — the deflection at a load is the partial derivative of strain energy with respect to it.
detail: **Unit load method** is its practical form: δ = Σ(PkL/AE) for trusses, ∫(Mm/EI)dx for beams. **Maxwell's reciprocal theorem**: the deflection at A due to a load at B equals that at B due to the same load at A.

fact: An **influence line** shows how a **function at one section** varies as a **unit load moves** across the span.
detail: Do not confuse it with a bending moment diagram, which shows the function **along the beam for a fixed load**. Influence lines are the basis of **moving load** analysis for bridges and gantry girders.

fact: **Degree of static indeterminacy D_s = r − 3** for a plane frame (r = number of reaction components), plus internal redundancy.
detail: General plane frame: **D_s = 3m + r − 3j**, and **kinematic indeterminacy D_k = 3j − r** (ignoring axial deformation, subtract the number of members). A propped cantilever is D_s = 1; a fixed beam D_s = 2.

fact: **Fixed end moments** for a UDL: **wL²/12** at each end. For a central point load: **WL/8**.
detail: These are the starting values for **moment distribution**. For a **propped** cantilever with UDL the support moment is **wL²/8**.

fact: **Moment distribution (Hardy Cross)**: distribute by **stiffness ratio**, carry over **half** to the far end if it is fixed.
detail: **Distribution factor = (I/L) of the member ÷ Σ(I/L) at the joint.** Carry-over factor is **½** to a fixed end and **0** to a hinged end. Relative stiffness of a member hinged at the far end is **¾(I/L)**.

fact: **Clapeyron's three-moment equation** relates the moments at three consecutive supports of a continuous beam.
detail: **M₁L₁ + 2M₂(L₁+L₂) + M₃L₂ = −6(A₁x̄₁/L₁ + A₂x̄₂/L₂)** for equal EI and level supports. Suits a continuous beam; moment distribution suits frames.

fact: **Slope-deflection: M_AB = (2EI/L)(2θ_A + θ_B − 3Δ/L) + FEM_AB.**
detail: The unknowns are **rotations and sway** — a **displacement (stiffness)** method, like the matrix stiffness method. Force methods (consistent deformation, three-moment) take **redundant forces** as unknowns instead.

fact: Indeterminate structures redistribute load and are **not affected by settlement, temperature or fabrication error** — determinate ones are.
detail: That is the key trade-off. Indeterminacy gives **redundancy** (alternative load paths, so one failure need not be collapse) but introduces **secondary stresses** from support settlement, temperature change and shrinkage.

fact: A **hinge (internal) transmits shear and axial force but NOT moment.**
detail: So the bending moment at an internal hinge is **always zero** — the single most useful equation in analysing a three-hinged arch or a hinged frame.

fact: **Thin cylinder: circumferential (hoop) stress = pd/2t; longitudinal = pd/4t.**
detail: Hoop stress is **twice** the longitudinal, so a cylindrical vessel splits along a **longitudinal seam**. **Thin sphere: pd/4t in every direction** — which is why a sphere is the most efficient pressure vessel. "Thin" means d/t > 20.

fact: **Shear centre** is the point through which a load must pass to cause **no twisting**.
detail: It coincides with the centroid for a **doubly symmetric** section. For a **channel** it lies **outside** the section, on the opposite side to the web — which is why a channel used as a purlin twists under a load applied at its centroid.

fact: A **cable** carries load in **pure tension**; the shape under a **UDL along the span** is a **parabola**, under **self-weight** a **catenary**.
detail: **Horizontal tension H = wL²/(8h)** — identical in form to the arch thrust, because a cable is an inverted arch. Maximum tension occurs **at the supports**, where the slope is steepest.

fact: IS 456 deflection limit: **span/depth ≤ 20 for simply supported, 26 continuous, 7 cantilever** (spans up to 10 m).
detail: These are the **deemed-to-satisfy** ratios that avoid an explicit deflection calculation. Beyond 10 m span they are multiplied by 10/span. Final deflection including creep and shrinkage is limited to **span/250**.

fact: **Portal frames** under lateral load: analyse by **portal method** (shear) or **cantilever method** (axial).
detail: **Portal method** assumes interior columns take twice the shear of exterior ones and suits **low-rise, wide** frames. **Cantilever method** distributes axial force by distance from the centroid and suits **tall, slender** frames.

fact: **Stress-strain curve for mild steel**: proportional limit → elastic limit → **upper and lower yield** → ultimate → **necking** → fracture.
detail: Mild steel shows a **distinct yield point**; **high-strength steel and concrete do not**, so a **0.2% proof stress** is used instead. The **breaking stress is lower than the ultimate** because of necking (on the nominal-area curve).

fact: **Combined bending and direct stress: σ = P/A ± M/Z.** No tension develops while **e ≤ d/6** for a rectangular section.
detail: This is the **middle-third rule**, and for a circular section the limit is **d/8**. It governs masonry dams, chimneys and retaining walls, where the material cannot take tension.

fact: **Method of tension coefficients** and the **graphical (Maxwell diagram)** method are alternatives for truss forces.
detail: In a roof truss under gravity load the **top chord (rafter) is in compression** and the **bottom chord (tie) in tension** — and the **king post is in TENSION**, hanging the tie beam from the apex.

fact: **Support reactions**: roller gives **1**, hinge **2**, fixed **3** unknowns in a plane structure.
detail: A plane structure is determinate when the total equals **3** (ΣH = ΣV = ΣM = 0). A roller permits rotation and translation along the surface; a hinge permits rotation only.

fact: The **matrix stiffness method** assembles member stiffness matrices into a global one: **[K]{D} = {F}**.
detail: It is the **displacement** method generalised, and the basis of all structural analysis software. The global stiffness matrix is **symmetric** and, after applying boundary conditions, **positive definite**.

fact: **Deflection is governed by EI (stiffness); strength by Z (section modulus).**
detail: Both must be checked separately: a section adequate in strength can fail the deflection limit, and often does for long, lightly loaded spans. That is why serviceability, not strength, sizes many beams.
